drapeaux.note: Article 62 of the Belgian Constitution (“le vote est obligatoire et secret”) is translated from the French; the official English translation was not retrieved. Original not retrieved.

The phrase “hardly ever prosecuted anymore” is French Wikipedia's wording (« quasiment plus jamais poursuivis »), translated here; French is the original language of the source, so this is a translation of French text.

titre: Compulsory Voting in Belgium (1893): A Rule Rarely Enforced
accroche: In Belgium, voting has been a constitutional obligation since 1893, but non-voters are now almost never prosecuted.
contenu_vulgarise:
On election day in Belgium, going to the polling station is not, in principle, a choice left to the voter: it is a legal obligation, written into the Constitution since 1893 for the election of the Chamber of Representatives, and not a mere civic encouragement. Article 62 of the current Constitution provides that “voting is compulsory and secret.” And yet, according to Wikipedia, non-voters have hardly ever been prosecuted since 2003.

## A Reform Born of Strikes and a Compromise

In 1893, after strikes that left people dead, the Belgian Parliament revised the Constitution. The compromise adopted replaced property-based suffrage with universal male suffrage, but **plural** suffrage: put forward by the deputies Albert Nyssens and Émile Féron, the text gave one vote to every man over 25, and up to two additional votes depending on one or two criteria: a secondary school diploma, the status of head of household over 35 paying at least 5 francs in residence tax, or a savings book of 2,000 francs (or an annuity of 100 francs). A single voter could thus have three votes. Women did not vote.

Voting was made compulsory the same year. The stated reason is not primarily punitive: it aims to allow all voters, and above all the poorest, to vote without pressure. An employer cannot set a workday on election day to keep his workers from going to the polls.

The figures for 1894, the first elections under the plural system, speak above all to the scale of the expansion of the suffrage: the electorate rose from 136,755 to 1,381,000 voters, and more than two million votes were counted, including those of voters with two or three votes. This rise comes from the new electoral system, not from the obligation to vote.

## An Obligation Rarely Enforced

Plural voting was applied from 1894 to 1918. The obligation to vote, for its part, remains in Article 62. The texts still provide penalties for the voter who abstains: a fine of €40 to €80, raised to €200 for a repeat offense, and, for anyone who fails to vote four times in fifteen years, removal from the electoral rolls for ten years. In practice, Wikipedia indicates that non-voters have been “hardly ever prosecuted anymore” since 2003: a political scientist counted about a dozen prosecutions in 2007, when nearly 690,000 Belgians had not voted. In March 2010, Justice Minister Stefaan De Clerck stated before a parliamentary committee that prosecuting abstainers was not a priority. A rule written into the Constitution can thus remain in force long after it has ceased to be enforced.

repere.texte: At the 1894 elections, the first under the plural voting system, the Belgian electorate rose from 136,755 to 1,381,000 voters, and more than two million votes were counted, according to the Senate as cited by Wikipedia.

carte.punch: In Belgium, voting has been compulsory since 1893, but almost no one is prosecuted anymore.
carte.idee: In 1893, Belgium made voting compulsory, the same year it widened the suffrage, so that everyone, especially the poorest, could vote without pressure from an employer. The rule remains in the Constitution, but non-voters have hardly ever been prosecuted since 2003.

quiz.question: Why was voting made compulsory in Belgium in 1893, the same year the suffrage was widened?
choix: To limit the number of parties allowed to run in elections
To replace plural voting with a strictly egalitarian vote
So that modest voters could vote without pressure from their employer
To grant women the right to vote at the same time as men
quiz.explication: The stated aim was to allow all voters, especially the poorest, to vote without pressure: an employer could not set a workday on election day. Plural voting was, on the contrary, established in 1893 and lasted until 1918, and women did not have the right to vote at that date.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who put forward the text of the 1893 Belgian constitutional revision, according to the entry?
choix: Stefaan De Clerck and Émile Féron
Leopold II and Stefaan De Clerck
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text of the 1893 revision was put forward by the deputies Albert Nyssens and Émile Féron, the entry specifies; Leopold II and Stefaan De Clerck play no part in adopting the text.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does a Belgian voter who fails to vote four times in fifteen years risk, according to the entry?
choix: Removal from the electoral rolls for ten years
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states that a voter who fails to vote four times in fifteen years faces removal from the electoral rolls for ten years, in addition to the fines provided for each abstention.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Justice Minister Stefaan De Clerck state before a parliamentary committee in March 2010, according to the entry?
choix: That prosecuting abstainers was not a priority
That the obligation to vote in Article 62 should be abolished
That the fines for abstainers should be doubled
That Belgium was going to abolish plural voting
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry reports that in March 2010, Stefaan De Clerck stated that prosecuting abstainers was not a priority, without announcing any reform of Article 62 or of plural voting, already abolished in 1918.
